newsitem.title: USA: Thomas remains controversial on U.S. Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Thomas remains controversial on U.S. Supreme Court.

text.p: Five years after Clarence Thomas sparked a national debate over sexual harassment, the conservative U.S. Supreme Court justice has emerged as one of the body's most provocative members.

On issues ranging from civil rights to abortion and the rights of criminal suspects, Thomas -- the second black to sit on the court, after the late Thurgood Marshall -- has joined Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justice Antonin Scalia on the panel's right wing.

At first bitter after the contentious 1991 Senate Judiciary Committee hearings, which led to his confirmation despite sexual harassment charges against him by University of Oklahoma law professor Anita Hill, a former legal assistant, Thomas has now mellowed, friends and observers say.
A longtime friend and conservative lawyer, Clint Bolick, said the criticism of Thomas has changed over the years.

"People attack him now as a Supreme Court justice, rather than the man involved in the Anita Hill controversy and an alleged sexual harasser. The focus has shifted, not the number of detractors," Bolick said.
He and other legal experts said Thomas had authored a number of conservative rulings that challenge the conventional view of the law, angering liberals and civil rights groups.

He has voted to restrict affirmative action programmes designed to help minorities overcome past discrimination, to strike down congressional districts drawn to increase the influence of minorities, and to oppose school desegregation.

His confirmation hearings turned memorably dramatic and acrimonious starting on Oct. 6, 1991, when Hill's harassment charges became public. Five days later the Senate Judiciary Committee held televised hearings over a weekend with Hill testifying and then Thomas defiantly denying her charges.
A secretary for Thomas said he does not grant any interviews -- standard policy for Supreme Court justices.
But in public speeches, Thomas has called the confirmation episode "a circus ... a national disgrace" and "illegitimate," although he has never discussed the allegations in detail.

Thomas said at a conservative, evangelical university in Virginia in May that it was "only by God's grace that my wife ... and I could have endured the unpleasantness of my confirmation. Our strategy was to rely on Him to endure the agony and then to transcend the aftermath of bitterness."
Representative Patricia Schroeder, who led a group of congresswomen on a march to the Senate to demand that Hill be heard, said Thomas's record has not surprised her.
"It is as pathetic as we thought it would be," said Schroeder, a liberal from Colorado. "Every day Clarence Thomas sits on the bench, she (Hill) feels more exonerated -- sadly but truly."

During her congressional testimony, Hill charged that Thomas had badgered her for dates and offended her with sexually explicit talk when he was her boss at the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in the early 1980s. She claimed he had talked to her about pornographic films, penis size and his prowess as a lover.
A furious Thomas denied all the charges.
He counter-charged racism and victimisation, denouncing the hearing as "a high-tech lynching for uppity blacks."

Members of the Senate Judiciary Committee said they could not decide whether Hill or Thomas was telling the truth. He won Senate approval by a 52-48 vote, receiving the largest number of negative votes ever for a successful Supreme Court nominee.
Armstrong Williams, a former aide and staunch defender, said Thomas has not mentioned the hearings in the past several years. "That's over. That's history. That's done," he said.

Williams, a conservative radio commentator, said Thomas seemed happy. "He is very into the job," Williams said, adding that the justice, who is 48, pointedly jokes about staying on the court for 40 years.
He said Thomas does not watch television news or read newspapers -- a practice adopted after the confirmation fight.
But Williams said Thomas stays updated on events in discussions with his wife Virginia, an aide to House of Representatives Republican Leader Dick Armey.
Thomas was nominated by President George Bush in 1991. He succeeded the legendary Marshall, a hero of early U.S. civil rights battles and a fierce champion of liberalism.
